actions.evaluations:
**Base UI** — Built by the creators of Radix, Floating UI, and Material UI, [`@base-ui/react` v1.9.0](https://github.com/mui/base-ui) delivers a clean, tree-shakable React headless primitive suite with compound part assembly (`Popover.Root`, `Positioner`, `Popup`), `useRender`/`mergeProps` composition, CSP/RTL providers, and modern viewport fixes such as iOS 26+ Safari backdrop handling documented in its [Quick Start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start). Its quality is high enough that both `shadcn/ui` and `Ouro UI` adopted it as their default web primitive layer, and its Markdown-per-page docs plus `llms.txt` serve coding agents well. However, it is deliberately unstyled (shipping zero design tokens or visual system), strictly React DOM web-only with no iOS, Android, or React Native rendering layer, and provides no runtime agent action/state bridge or generative UI protocol. Pairing it with a cross-platform token/component system and a runtime agent interface layer—which is effectively what Ouro UI builds on top of it—addresses those gaps, so I would use Base UI underneath a broader system rather than as my standalone choice.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's [`microsoft/fluentui`](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) monorepo houses three web libraries: [Fluent UI React v9](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui/blob/master/packages/react-components/react-components/README.md) (`@fluentui/react-components`, built on slot-based JSX APIs, `FluentProvider` token themes, and Griffel atomic CSS-in-JS), legacy React v8, and FAST-based [Fluent UI Web Components](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui/blob/master/packages/web-components/README.md) with Declarative Shadow DOM templates and Custom Elements Manifests. While battle-tested across Microsoft 365 web apps, `microsoft/fluentui` itself is web-only (Microsoft's Apple, Android, and alpha React Native Fluent toolkits live in separate repositories with divergent APIs), its fonts and icons carry separate Microsoft asset license restrictions outside MIT, Griffel style objects add friction for coding agents trained primarily on standard CSS/Tailwind, and it includes no runtime agent action layer, WebMCP bridge, or generative UI protocol. Unifying web and native primitives under a single cross-platform token/component contract and exposing typed agent actions alongside slot UIs would address my core objections.

**A2UI** — [`a2ui-project/a2ui`](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui) defines an Apache-2.0 streaming generative UI protocol ([v1.0 specification](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/)) that separates UI topology (`createSurface` and flat adjacency-list `updateComponents` for focus-preserving incremental patches) from state (`updateDataModel` with JSON Pointer `@path` two-way bindings and bidirectional `callRendererFunction`/`callAgentFunction` RPC), backed by [official renderers and Agent SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) across React, Lit, Angular, Flutter (`a2ui_flutter`), SwiftUI (`A2UISwiftUI`), and Jetpack Compose ([`androidx.a2ui` 1.0.0-alpha02](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/a2ui), currently implementing v0.9.1). It is the strongest cross-platform wire standard when an agent needs to stream dynamic UI to a human without executing untrusted code. However, A2UI is a generative wire protocol and catalog adapter, not a design system or full-application toolkit: v1.0 explicitly stripped `theme` properties from `createSurface` so visual styling, tokens, static app shells, and accessible primitives must come from a separate host design system, and it only models agent-to-human view generation rather than giving agents structured interfaces (CLI, MCP, App Intents, AppFunctions) to operate an application. Bringing Compose up to v1.0 and pairing A2UI with a full HX/AX design system addresses this, making A2UI an ideal companion protocol rather than my primary design system.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — [`BuilderIO/agent-native`](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native) gets a foundational architectural principle right in its [framework documentation](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/): a single Zod-typed `defineAction` powers React UI hooks (`useActionQuery`), agent tools, HTTP endpoints, CLI, MCP, and A2A over shared PostgreSQL/PGlite state and UI context so agents work through the same permissioned action layer rather than clicking buttons. It also bundles [`@agent-native/toolkit`](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/toolkit/package.json) (shadcn-style React/Tailwind UI, app shells, collaboration, and sandboxed Alpine.js generative UI). The trade-off is that it is an opinionated full-stack server/application framework coupled to Node 22.22+, Nitro, and Postgres rather than a portable cross-platform design system: its [`desktop-app`](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/desktop-app/package.json) is an Electron wrapper, its Expo [`mobile-app`](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/mobile-app/package.json) is a `"private": true` internal app rather than a published native component kit, and it lacks cross-platform DTCG design tokens, native SwiftUI/Compose controls, or automated visual/AX conformance checks verifying UI-to-action parity. Decoupling the shared action/UI layer into a framework-agnostic design toolkit with public native component packages and parity verification would address those limits.

**Tamagui** — [`tamagui/tamagui`](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui) is one of the strongest universal human UI systems for React Web and React Native, combining `@tamagui/core` tokens and hierarchical sub-tree `<Theme>` switching, `<Adapt>` primitives that morph desktop popovers into native touch sheets, and the `@tamagui/static` optimizing compiler that flattens styled components into atomic CSS + `div` on web and hoisted style objects + `View` on iOS/Android, alongside detailed [`llms.txt` documentation](https://tamagui.dev/llms.txt) for coding agents. Where it falls short for this brief is an observed total gap on the runtime agent side: Tamagui ships no agent action/state bridge, no CLI/MCP/WebMCP/App Intents/AppFunctions integration, no generative UI catalog, and no agentic interaction patterns. Its static compiler (`tamagui.build.ts`) also requires exact lockstep versions across `@tamagui/*` packages and Node-time partial evaluation rules that frequently trip coding agents when mixing dynamic modules, while `html.*` strict-DOM elements remain in early development. Adding a cross-platform typed action/agent-bridge layer and relaxing build-time static evaluation pitfalls would make Tamagui far more competitive here.

**Chakra UI** — In v3 (`@chakra-ui/react` v3.38.0), [`chakra-ui/chakra-ui`](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui) modernized its architecture around [`@ark-ui/react` state machines and `@emotion/react`](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui/blob/main/packages/react/package.json) with Panda-aligned [CSS `@layer` cascade recipes](https://chakra-ui.com/llms-styling.txt) (`reset, base, tokens, recipes`), `createSystem` token theming, `asChild` polymorphism, RSC compatibility, CLI `typegen`, and `@chakra-ui/react-mcp` plus `llms-full.txt` for coding agents. Despite strong human accessibility and developer ergonomics on React web, Chakra UI is strictly React DOM web-only with zero native iOS, Android, or React Native targets, retains a runtime `@emotion/react` CSS-in-JS dependency, and limits its agent story to coding-agent documentation lookup (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) with no runtime agent interfaces, WebMCP tool exposure, or generative UI primitives. Shipping zero-runtime cross-platform token/component targets and a runtime agent state/action layer would be needed to address these trade-offs.

**json-render** — Vercel Labs' [`vercel-labs/json-render`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render) is a remarkably versatile Apache-2.0 generative UI framework: developers define Zod-typed component and action schemas (`defineCatalog`), generate LLM system prompts (`catalog.prompt()`), stream progressive JSON/YAML element maps (`SpecStream`) with reactive `$state`, `$cond`, `$template`, `$computed`, and `watch` bindings, and render across 30 packages spanning React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, `@json-render/shadcn` (36 components), `@json-render/react-native` (25+ mobile components), terminal (`ink`), chat cards, MCP Apps, PDF, email, Remotion video, and Three.js. However, `json-render` is a spec-to-component generative projection layer rather than a foundational design system: it delegates web accessibility and styling to shadcn/Radix + Tailwind and mobile rendering to basic React Native views (with no native SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose renderers and no unified cross-platform design token pipeline), its flat JSON expression DSL hits an expressiveness ceiling for bespoke human UX compared with real component code, and it only handles agents rendering views for people rather than agents operating app capabilities directly. Pairing it with unified cross-platform design tokens, native SwiftUI/Compose catalogs, and bidirectional agent-consumable action schemas would address those gaps.

**Radix UI** — [`radix-ui/primitives`](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives) pioneered unstyled, accessible React compound primitives (`Slot`/`asChild`, roving focus, modal dismissal layers, and WAI-ARIA compliance) and remains actively maintained under WorkOS, with [2026 releases](https://radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/releases) adding React 19 ref-loop fixes, tree-shakable subpath exports (`radix-ui/accordion`), and `unstable_BubbleInput` form composition. Even so, Radix Primitives is strictly unstyled (requiring a separate token/styling layer), strictly React DOM web-only with zero native mobile or desktop support, and offers no agent-facing runtime APIs, structured coding-agent self-correction diagnostics, or generative UI support. Notably, Radix's original creators moved on to build Base UI, and `shadcn/ui` switched its default foundation from Radix to Base UI in July 2026. Addressing these objections would require cross-platform token/native primitives and a structured runtime agent contract, which Radix Primitives explicitly leaves out of scope.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Apple's [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines), and [App Intents framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) represent the gold standard for single-vendor native integration across iOS, iPadOS (including 2026 iPhone Duo foldable posture guidance and Liquid Glass materials), macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and visionOS. Crucially, `Button(_:intent:)`, `AppEntity`, `requestConfirmation()`, and the Siri AI Developer Preview unify human touch controls and system/agent execution over one typed intent graph with OS-enforced permissions, VoiceOver rotors, and Dynamic Type. The decisive trade-off is hard platform lock-in: SwiftUI cannot target the Web, Android, Windows, or Linux at all, forcing teams building web-and-native software to maintain an entirely separate design system, component library, and MCP/web agent layer elsewhere. Only cross-platform web/Android targets (which Apple has no reason to ship) would resolve that, making SwiftUI best consumed as the native Apple rendering substrate of a cross-platform token and claim system like Ouro UI.

**CopilotKit** — [`CopilotKit/CopilotKit`](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit) is a comprehensive MIT-licensed agentic application middleware and chat/copilot framework built around the event-driven AG-UI 1.0 protocol, connecting Python/TS/Go/.NET backends (LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, Google ADK, PydanticAI) to [frontend packages](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/tree/main/packages) across React, Angular, Vue, Web Components, [`@copilotkit/react-native`](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/blob/main/packages/react-native/package.json), and Slack/Teams/Discord/WhatsApp channels. It excels at `useAgent` shared state, human-in-the-loop tool approvals, WebMCP registration, and supporting all three generative UI paradigms simultaneously (controlled app components, `@copilotkit/a2ui-renderer` for A2UI 1.0, and `@copilotkit/mcp-apps-renderer` for MCP Apps). However, CopilotKit is an embedded copilot and protocol orchestration stack, not a foundational design system or general-purpose UI primitive library: you still must bring your own design tokens, buttons, forms, tables, and navigation shells for the human application, its native mobile support is limited to React Native copilot/sheet surfaces (requiring stream/DOM polyfills) rather than native SwiftUI or Compose widget kits, and production durability/analytics/hosted channels push toward commercial `CopilotKit Intelligence`. Pairing CopilotKit with a true cross-platform design system addresses its UI toolkit gap, so it complements rather than replaces a design system.

**Flutter** — Google's [`flutter/flutter`](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) compiles Dart to native ARM machine code and WebAssembly/JS while painting every pixel through its own hardware-accelerated Impeller/Skia engine across iOS, Android, Web, Windows, macOS, and Linux, shipping comprehensive Material and Cupertino widget sets, explicit [`Semantics` accessibility trees](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility-and-internationalization/accessibility), and first-party A2UI v1.0 generative UI via `a2ui_flutter` (which officially replaced the now-discontinued [`genui` package](https://pub.dev/packages/genui)). Its core trade-off is canvas isolation: on the web, rendering to a custom canvas/Wasm surface instead of semantic HTML/DOM degrades native browser text/layout idioms, SEO, bundle startup weight, and interoperability with DOM-based browser agents and WebMCP (`document.modelContext`); on native platforms, it requires Dart + platform channels/FFI to bridge iOS App Intents or Android AppFunctions rather than sharing TypeScript/Swift/Kotlin ecosystems; and it provides no built-in AX CLI/MCP action contract for agents operating the app without UI. Semantic DOM compilation on web and first-class multi-platform agent intent/MCP projection from Dart actions would address my main objections.

**AI Elements** — [`vercel/ai-elements`](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) provides copy-in React/Next.js components (`Message`, `Conversation`, `Reasoning`, `CodeBlock`) built atop `shadcn/ui` and the Vercel AI SDK for rendering conversational AI streams. Its disqualifying documented fact is an explicit deprecation banner at the top of its repository README: the project is scheduled for deprecation at the end of November 2026 and superseded by [AI Elements in `shadcn/ui`](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) (which dropped low-usage wrappers such as `artifact`, `canvas`, and `jsx-preview` during the October 2026 migration). Even setting deprecation aside, it covers only human-facing chat/output widgets (not a complete application design system), is locked to Next.js/React web + CSS-variables Tailwind + Vercel AI SDK with zero native mobile/desktop support, and exposes no runtime interfaces for agents to operate the app. Because upstream has officially folded it into `shadcn/ui`, there is no reason to adopt standalone `vercel/ai-elements` for new work.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Google's [Material 3 for Jetpack Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) pairs declarative Kotlin UI with dynamic tonal color schemes, M3 Expressive motion/shapes, adaptive navigation (`NavigationBar`, `NavigationRail`, `NavigationDrawer`), and two major 2026 agentic building blocks on Android: [`androidx.a2ui` (`1.0.0-alpha02`)](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/a2ui) for rendering A2UI agent surfaces natively into Compose without arbitrary code execution, and [`androidx.appfunctions` (`1.0.0-rc01`)](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/appfunctions) for exposing typed on-device tools aligned with MCP naming conventions (`instructions`) via KSP. The trade-off is that first-party Jetpack Compose M3 is Android-centric: extending it to Web and iOS via JetBrains Compose Multiplatform draws onto a Skia/Wasm canvas rather than semantic HTML/DOM on the web or native SwiftUI/Liquid Glass idioms on Apple platforms, imposes Google's opinionated Material visual identity, and `androidx.a2ui` remains in `alpha02` trailing the A2UI v1.0 spec at v0.9.1. Stabilizing `androidx.a2ui` at v1.0 and pairing Android Compose/AppFunctions with native web DOM and SwiftUI counterparts via shared DTCG tokens would address its cross-platform limitations.

**MCP Apps** — [`modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps) is the official Model Context Protocol extension (`2026-01-26` stable spec) allowing MCP servers to attach `ui://` HTML resources (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`) to tools and render interactive views inline inside sandboxed iframes over `PostMessageTransport` JSON-RPC across Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose, and Postman, with `useHostStyles` forwarding host CSS variables/fonts. While valuable as a cross-host protocol for interactive tool widgets inside AI chats, MCP Apps is an iframe embedding transport, not a design system or component toolkit: it ships zero UI components of its own (requiring you to bring React, Vue, Svelte, or vanilla UI kits inside each bundle), isolates every surface inside web iframes (incurring heavy overhead for fine-grained UI and relying on WebViews rather than native controls on mobile), and cannot build standalone web or native applications. Shipping or pairing with a full cross-platform component/token system is mandatory, so MCP Apps is a host-integration target rather than a foundational UI toolkit.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Adobe's [`adobe/react-spectrum`](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum) monorepo sets an industry benchmark for human accessibility and internationalization across [React Aria](https://react-aria.adobe.com/) (50+ unstyled components and hooks normalizing mouse, touch, keyboard, focus rings, virtualized collections, and screen-reader announcements across 30+ languages and 13 calendar systems), React Stately, and [React Spectrum](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/) (implementing Adobe's Spectrum 2 design system). However, `react-aria-components` and `@react-spectrum/s2` render exclusively to React DOM on the web: although `react-stately` hooks avoid DOM globals in principle, Adobe ships no React Native, SwiftUI, or Jetpack Compose rendering primitives or cross-platform mobile tokens. Furthermore, React Spectrum enforces Adobe's corporate visual language while React Aria's render-prop/slot composition is unstyled and more verbose for coding agents than props-first registries, and neither includes any runtime agent action/state bridge, WebMCP tool exposure, or generative UI layer. Official native mobile/desktop renderers and a typed agent capability surface alongside `react-stately` state machines would address those gaps.

**MUI** — [`mui/material-ui`](https://github.com/mui/material-ui) (`@mui/material`, with [`master` advancing toward v10 alpha](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/blob/master/packages/mui-material/package.json) alongside `MUI X` data grids, charts, and pickers) offers unmatched enterprise React web component breadth and ten years of production hardening, plus optional zero-runtime CSS extraction via `@mui/material-pigment-css`. Its trade-offs for greenfield human-and-agent cross-platform work are substantial: `@mui/material` is strictly React DOM web-only with zero native iOS, Android, or React Native components; its default aesthetic remains anchored to Material Design 2 unless heavily overridden; transitioning between runtime Emotion (`sx`/styled) and build-time Pigment CSS introduces ecosystem split and verbose override boilerplate that bloats coding-agent context windows; and it provides zero runtime agent bridges, MCP/CLI action contracts, or generative UI primitives. Even MUI's own team created `@base-ui/react` for clean headless web foundations; adding cross-platform native primitives, DTCG token parity, and first-class agent interfaces would be required to change my verdict here.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — [`openai/apps-sdk-ui`](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) provides an MIT-licensed React 18/19 + Tailwind CSS v4 + Radix library of [29 component directories](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/tree/main/src/components) (`Alert`, `Badge`, `Button`, `CodeBlock`, `DateRangePicker`, `Markdown`, `Menu`, `Popover`, `Select`, `ShimmerText`, etc.) and tokens crafted specifically for inline apps inside ChatGPT. Its scope is intentionally narrow: it lacks core full-application primitives (such as `Dialog`, `Sheet`, `Tabs`, data `Table`, full `Form` architecture, or app navigation shells), is strictly React web-only with zero native iOS or Android rendering, visually conforms to ChatGPT's host chrome rather than serving as a brandable cross-platform design system, and couples to a single vendor host ecosystem (so much so that `modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps` ships a `migrate-oai-app` skill to migrate apps off the OpenAI Apps SDK to open MCP Apps). Expanding to a vendor-neutral full component catalog with native platform targets and agent-consumable action APIs would be necessary to use it as a primary toolkit.

**shadcn/ui** — [`shadcn-ui/ui`](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui) transformed web UI distribution with its open-code flat-file registry (`npx shadcn`, `registry.json`, private registries, and an official MCP Server for coding agents), and its [2026 releases](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/changelog) expanded [`ui.shadcn.com`](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs) to support Base UI (default since July 2026), React Aria, and Radix across eight visual styles on Tailwind CSS v4, alongside `@shadcn/helpers/ai-sdk` human-in-the-loop mocking and 21 first-party [AI Elements](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) (`Trace`, `Message`, `Questionnaire`, `Code Block`). For React web human interfaces authored by coding agents, its transparency is superb. Yet two concrete gaps prevent it from being my overall pick: first, it is strictly React DOM web-only, with zero SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, or React Native components or cross-platform DTCG token compilation; second, its AI features focus on coding-agent installation and rendering chat/traces *to people*, offering zero runtime agent interfaces (no CLI/MCP/WebMCP/App Intents action layer) and no automated visual/accessibility/jank verifier after agents edit copied-in files. Adding a cross-platform token/native tier and an agent-facing runtime contract—which Ouro UI builds directly on top of the `shadcn` CLI registry format—would address both objections.

**Vercel UI SDK** — [`vercel-labs/ui`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui) (`@ui-sdk/core` plus React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Component adapters) tackles both coding-agent component authoring (`definePrimitive`, `createParts`, composable focus/selection/popup/drag-and-drop behaviors, and bundled Markdown skills) and [in-page runtime agent operation](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents) via `@ui-sdk/*/agent` (`createAgent`, `agent.snapshot()`, `agent.act()`, `allow` guards, `source: "agent"` change attribution, agent-scoped undo history, and [WebMCP `document.modelContext` tool registration](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/webmcp)). Its benchmarked reduction in browser-agent tool calls and token reads is compelling. However, it is in `0.1.0-beta` with unstable APIs, is completely unstyled/headless (shipping zero design tokens or visual theme system), targets web DOM exclusively with zero native iOS, Android, or React Native support, and restricts runtime agents to driving mounted DOM controls (and Chromium's experimental WebMCP API) rather than exposing headless CLI, server MCP, or native OS intent surfaces when no browser tab is open. Graduating to 1.0, pairing with a cross-platform token/visual system, and projecting primitive actions to non-DOM/native agent surfaces would address those limitations.

**Ouro UI** — [`ourostack/ouro-ui`](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui) is the candidate I would choose because its entire architecture is built around the exact dual-consumer, multi-platform premise of this evaluation: **Ouro HX** for interfaces people use and **Ouro AX** for interfaces agents use, united by [`ouro-ui-core`](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core) (DTCG 2025.10 tokens compiled via Terrazzo with SHA-256 byte-for-byte parity into Tailwind CSS v4 on web and zero-dependency `OuroTokens.swift` on Apple, plus machine-checkable component and interaction-feel claims). On web (`v1.3.14`), Ouro HX ships ~115 React 19 + Base UI components via the `shadcn` registry format with props-first APIs, layout-only `className` guards that emit `[ouro-ui] <Component>: ... Fix: <exact code>` diagnostics, `Porthole`/`portholeStatus` shared human/agent JSON state, `AgentPresence`, and `ouro-check` (headless Playwright + axe-core verification across 320px–3840px light/dark catching overlap, contrast, typography-scale drift, leaked `undefined`/`NaN`, and jank without screenshots). On native Apple, [`ourostack/ouro-ui-apple`](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) (`v0.3.x`) ships SwiftUI `OuroHX` tokens/motion/haptics/foldable posture (`OuroFoldReader`), `OuroFeel` simulator jank checks, and [`OuroReins`](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple/blob/main/docs/ouro-reins/README.md) (~19ms headless `ls`/`do` node-tree driving). actions.testimonial: I would choose Ouro UI because it designs human interfaces (Ouro HX) and agent interfaces (Ouro AX) as co-equal, contract-verified halves of one system rather than forcing agents to scrape or click through human screens. Its React/Base UI and SwiftUI layers compile byte-for-byte DTCG tokens from ouro-ui-core while ouro-check, OuroFeel, and OuroReins verify layout, accessibility, and interaction jank headlessly with structured JSON diagnostics instead of screenshot guesswork. On the runtime-agent side, ax-command, ax-outcome, and ax-wait turn a single command definition into CLI and MCP surfaces with checked postconditions, resumable cursors, and --why/--dry-run safety gates, all audited from the outside by ax-xray and ouro-ax-xray across web and Apple App Intents. The honest trade-off against Tamagui or Flutter is native breadth today—ouro-ui-apple is still pre-release with only five OuroHX components and Ouro UI has no Android target yet—but extending its clean token-and-claim pipeline to additional native views is far more tractable than retrofitting disciplined agent semantics and black-box conformance onto a human-only UI toolkit.
